rv.q: But the indispensable big fish of these proceedings is one Norbert Leo Butz, who truly does all you could reasonably ask of an actor in such a musical.
The show's saving grace is that it knows what it wants to be: a feel-good musical about the importance of family, told with enough theatrical razzle-dazzle to sugar-coat its bitter pill of mortality.
So when audience members around me were dabbing their eyes through the protracted finale, why did I want to take a shower?

While acknowledging that the show is about a self-consciously rambling and absurdist hero, the bloated 90-minute Act 1 threatens to derail as visual gags, projections and busy scenes - plus a book that uneasily mixes whimsy and cancer - bombard the senses....
Yet the show is hobbled by a major flaw: Andrew Lippa’s thoroughly mediocre score.
Unfortunately, Andrew Lippa’s score is a hack job stringing one banal non-tune after another.
So it's crushing to realize, early on, that this gentle, sincere, beautiful-looking show is deadly dull.
Not once did I feel that what I was seeing had been spawned by the teeming mind of Edward Bloom.
Despite a heartfelt performance by Norbert Leo Butz and a lovely score by Andrew Lippa, this adaptation of Daniel Wallace's novel never finds its theatrical footing.
But the show built around him is a pulseless bore, and you can see his shoulders sagging from carrying all that weight.
For the most part, though, Big Fish finds theatrically inventive ways to reel audiences into its central love story.
Broadway’s new musical fable, “Big Fish,” is a singing version of catch-and-release.
Where “Big Fish” gets stuck in the shallows is with its score, by Andrew Lippa (“The Addams Family”).

As the sequences of Edward's fantasies play out, however, the father-son story is frequently lost in the whimsicality rather than enhanced by it. It's only near the very end, when Will learns what Edward has accomplished and comes to appreciate the value of a man telling stories, that all the elements properly converge.
In the end, though, this Big Fish lacks the imagination or cohesion to reel you in like one of its hero's yarns.
Suddenly, they’re not archetypes anymore but rather the stars of some “Best of Broadway” theme-park show.
Stroman, at the top of her game, whips this warmhearted story into a supremely imaginative and heart-tugging entertainment.
But the biggest fish in this pond is Butz, who splashes and swims with grace, confidence, and charisma.
